The phase detector used on the PC130-438 circuit card is a
tri-state, sequential device. Its job is to compare the reference frequency against the incoming frequency of the VCO.

The output voltage generated by sequential phase detectors is the result of the time interval between the zero crossing of the two frequencies. With the memory capability of sequential detectors, they can provide phase detection characteristics not normally obtainable when multiplier circuits are used.
Sequential phase detectors are normally designed using digital circuits and, in effect, have memory. This is not true with multipliers which are zero-memory devices.
A well designed multiplier is capable of phase-lock on signals in noisy environments.

SYNTHESIS - The term "synthesis" refers to any process in which separate elements are combined to form a coherent whole. Frequency synthesis generates a large number of stable frequencies (within a pre-established range) using only a few oscillators. In most cases, only one oscillator is required.

An AM signal from a broadcast station carrying voice or music is much more complicated. The AM waveform in that case is more complex as it must, by design, display the many varied frequencies and amplitudes of the audio signal.

The illustration below shows a portion of an amplitude modulated signal made up of carrier frequency modulated by a single sinusoidal wave. Maximum and minimum amplitudes (Emax and Emin) are easily defined in this example.

When the sidebands cross themselves, a great deal of distortion occurs and can cause the signal to be completely unintelligible.
The amplitude of an AM waveform may never be allowed to exceed half the carrier amplitude. If this happens, the two sidebands (USB & LSB) cross themselves at Emin.
This AM bouncing phenomena compels the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to limit many AM broadcast stations to operation only during hours of daylight.
Because of this, the normal operating range (during daylight) for an AM broadcast station transmitting at 50 kwatts is up to
200 miles because the transmission is limited to ground-wave coverage.

FM transmissions are a much higher frequency which allows the transmitted waves to penetrate the atmosphere and enter outer space. Consequently, FM signals never stray from their assigned coverage area.

A listener in that coverage area would now tune to two stations on one frequency. Depending on the signal strength, sensitivity, selectivity and position of the receiver, one or the other or both of the stations will be heard.
For AM radio this is a problem because rogue signals entering a neighboring coverage area may be at the same frequency of another transmitter.
This propagation characteristic of sky waves is extremely useful for short-wave radio which uses the atmospheric bouncing to an advantage.
This allows AM signals to bounce off the F1 layer which permits the signals to randomly bounce thousands of miles out of their assigned coverage area.
The earth's ionosphere is made up of several layers. The inner-most layers (D & E) dissipate during hours of darkness.
This characteristic of radio waves can sometimes be a problem for AM signals.
Radio frequencies have a tendency to bounce off the ionosphere and earth. This is predictable and, in most instances, desirable.
A more realistic view of an AM signal sampled by a spectrum analyzer displays all the frequencies associated with the intelligence being transmitted.

Once the carrier signal has been modulated, the information is now located on the upper and lower sidebands of the composite signal which contains: the original carrier, the sum of the carrier and modulator, and the difference of the carrier and modulator.

With amplitude modulation, information is "encoded" into the carrier wave by varying the RF carrier's amplitude with the variations of the audio wave which contains the information, while maintaining constant frequency.

It wasn't until the 1st World War that the true benefits of wireless communications became evident. Commanders were able to monitor distant elements of their commands and provide instructions to subordinate commanders without leaving the command post. From here, radio soon grew to the giant it is today.

In the early part of this century, the telegraph reigned. It is likely that the time, money and effort that went into providing telegraph service nation-wide was the major factor that inhibited the acceptance of wireless communications.

Voice transmissions were achieved through the use of modulating radio frequencies with the information to be transmitted. Not only did modulating carrier frequencies allow for voice transmissions by radio, but also paved the way for telephone, which also uses modulation.
INTRODUCTIONM
Between the late 1800's and the early 1900's, "wireless" communication technology moved rapidly. It was logical for radio to move from the realm of transmitted code to actual voice transmissions.
